write.desc: The real numbers treated axiomatically as a complete ordered field: the algebra of order and absolute value, how to handle inequalities in proofs, supremum and infimum, the completeness axiom and its first consequences (Archimedean property, density, square roots, nested intervals, uncountability). The points belong together because they all describe what the reals are and what completeness lets us prove about them, which every later existence theorem relies on.

points.name: The reals as an ordered field
points.what: The learner can state the field and order axioms of the real numbers and use them to prove basic facts such as 0 < 1, a^2 >= 0, and that multiplying an inequality by a negative number reverses it. They see that the rationals satisfy the same axioms, so something more is needed to single out the reals.
outside: direct proof and proof by contradiction

points.name: Absolute value and the triangle inequality
points.what: The learner can work with |x| by cases, interpret |x - a| as distance, prove the triangle inequality |a + b| <= |a| + |b| and its reverse form ||a| - |b|| <= |a - b|, and rewrite |x - a| < r as a - r < x < a + r.

points.name: Working with inequalities in proofs
points.what: The learner can bound expressions step by step, reduce a goal by 'it suffices to show', and use the trick that if a <= b + epsilon for every epsilon > 0 then a <= b (and if |a - b| < epsilon for every epsilon > 0 then a = b).
outside: quantifiers 'for all' and 'there exists' and negating them

points.name: Upper and lower bounds
points.what: The learner can decide whether a subset of the reals is bounded above or below, find upper and lower bounds, and tell a maximum or minimum of a set apart from a mere bound, with examples such as open and closed intervals and {1/n}.

points.name: Supremum and infimum
points.what: The learner can state the definition of the supremum as the least upper bound (and the infimum as the greatest lower bound), prove that a supremum is unique, compute sup and inf of simple sets, and explain that the supremum need not belong to the set.

points.name: The completeness axiom
points.what: The learner can state the least upper bound property, understand it as the one axiom that separates the reals from the rationals, and deduce from it that every nonempty set bounded below has an infimum (via inf A = -sup(-A)).

points.name: The epsilon characterisation of the supremum
points.what: The learner can prove and use the fact that an upper bound s of A is the supremum exactly when for every epsilon > 0 there is an element of A greater than s - epsilon, together with the matching statement for the infimum.

points.name: Proving facts about sup and inf
points.what: The learner can prove properties of suprema and infima directly from the definition, such as sup(A + B) = sup A + sup B, sup(cA) = c sup A for c > 0, A subset of B implies sup A <= sup B, and inf A <= sup A, using either the definition or the epsilon characterisation.

points.name: The Archimedean property
points.what: The learner can prove from completeness that the natural numbers are not bounded above, and use the equivalent form that for every epsilon > 0 there is n with 1/n < epsilon, which later supplies the N in limit proofs.

points.name: Density of the rationals and irrationals
points.what: The learner can prove that between any two real numbers there is a rational number and an irrational number, and use density to approximate any real number by rationals.
outside: well-ordering of the natural numbers or induction

points.name: Existence of square roots
points.what: The learner can prove that there is a real number whose square is 2 by taking the supremum of {x : x^2 < 2} and ruling out both s^2 < 2 and s^2 > 2, and see why the same set has no supremum in the rationals. The argument extends to n-th roots of positive numbers.

points.name: The nested interval property
points.what: The learner can prove directly from the supremum that a decreasing chain of closed bounded intervals has a nonempty intersection, and give examples showing that it fails for open intervals or for the rationals.
outside: indexed unions and intersections of sets

points.name: The reals are uncountable
points.what: The learner can prove that the real numbers (and any interval) are uncountable using nested intervals, and relate this to Cantor's diagonal argument on decimal expansions.

points.name: The extended reals as notation
points.what: The learner can read and use the symbols plus and minus infinity as notation, for example sup A = +infinity for a set not bounded above and intervals such as (a, infinity), knowing they are not real numbers and cannot be used in arithmetic as if they were.

points.name: Where the reals come from
points.what: The learner knows that the reals can be constructed from the rationals (by Dedekind cuts or by Cauchy sequences) and that any two complete ordered fields are essentially the same, so working from the axioms loses nothing.
